planting.note: Divide basal offshoots or plant nursery starts in spring in a rich, well-drained potting mix, kept in deep to partial shade; the wild species is the plain dark-green-leaved parent behind the variegated 'Curtisii' selection and performs equally well in low interior light.

directions: Aglaonema nitidum is a clumping understory aroid native to the lowland rainforests of Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, and Borneo, bearing broad, glossy, deep-green lance-shaped leaves on short stems. It tolerates deep interior shade and dim, north-facing rooms better than almost any other large-leaved foliage plant, though it also accepts bright indirect light without issue. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, protect from temperatures below 55 degrees Fahrenheit and cold drafts, and avoid direct sun, which scorches the leaves. As with other aroids, the sap contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause mouth and throat irritation if chewed, so keep it away from pets and small children.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix in spring, or plant nursery starts; grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, fertile potting mix; in zones 10-11 it can be grown outdoors in shaded, humus-rich beds.

directions: Dieffenbachia maculata is a tropical American aroid prized for its broad, glossy, cane-like stems topped with large leaves irregularly blotched and speckled in cream, white, and pale green over a darker green background, the wild form behind many of the named dumb cane cultivars grown as houseplants. Grow it in bright, indirect light to partial shade, since direct sun bleaches and scorches the variegated foliage, and keep the potting mix lightly moist, letting the top inch dry between waterings. It prefers warmth and humidity and declines below 60 degrees Fahrenheit, so keep it away from cold drafts and drying heat vents. All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense burning, swelling, and temporary loss of speech if chewed, hence the common name "dumb cane"; wear gloves when pruning or propagating and keep it away from children and pets.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Pot rooted stem cuttings or nursery starts in spring in well-drained potting mix; this slow-growing dracaena establishes best when repotted during warm, actively growing months.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in a shaded tropical garden bed, since direct sun scorches the glossy, deep-green, narrow leaves that whorl densely around slender, sparsely branching canes. Water when the top couple of inches of potting mix dry out, letting the plant approach dryness between waterings rather than sitting wet, and use a well-drained, slightly acidic mix. It tolerates average indoor humidity and temperatures but dislikes cold drafts below 55 degrees F, and over years develops into an upright, multi-stemmed small tree valued for its architectural form. As with other dracaenas, the foliage is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed or ingested, causing vomiting and drooling.
